title: Crossover from Fast Scrambling to Operator Confinement Tuned by an Auxiliary Qubit
authors: Ryan Buechele, Joseph Szabo, Nandini Trivedi
abstract: We demonstrate a static, disorder-free spin chain Hamiltonian which, by tuning the coupling to an auxiliary qubit, realizes a crossover between super-ballistic, ancilla-accelerated scrambling and sub-ballistic operator confinement. Our minimal model is the mixed-field Ising chain with a spin-1/2 ancilla coupled to its longitudinal magnetization. The ancilla mediates an effective all-to-all interaction which accelerates operator spreading and entanglement growth when weakly coupled, but rapidly saturates its entanglement and projects spin chain operators into effectively frozen subspaces when the ancilla coupling is strong. We locate this crossover independently through both a divergent peak in the mutual-information saturation time near $λ_c N/h \approx 8$ and an exponential suppression of the late-time OTOC growth rate, $\logα\propto 1/λ$. Through a Feshbach-Fano projection and Schrieffer-Wolff transformation, we reveal an effective hidden symmetry on the chain which confines operators on the chain for a time exponential in the coupling strength. This reconciles the fast, $\log(N)$ scrambling reported for random-unitary-circuit realizations of the star geometry with the confinement previously found in its time-independent Hamiltonian analog, showing both emerge from a single Hamiltonian family as a function of one dimensionless parameter.
summary: The authors present a minimal spin chain model coupled to an ancilla qubit whose coupling strength ($\lambda$) acts as a control knob. By tuning $\lambda$, the system undergoes a controlled crossover from rapid, scrambling dynamics to slow operator confinement. This work is significant because it shows that such fundamentally different quantum behaviors can emerge from a single Hamiltonian structure.
main_problem: The study investigates how tuning an auxiliary qubit coupling can induce a crossover between fast, super-ballistic quantum scrambling and slow, sub-ballistic operator confinement in a time-independent Hamiltonian system.
main_result: The model successfully demonstrates this transition within a single Hamiltonian family by controlling the ancilla coupling strength ($\lambda$), revealing an effective hidden symmetry responsible for confinement at strong coupling.
method: The analysis employs advanced quantum information diagnostics, including Von Neumann entropy, Mutual Information, and Out-of-Time-Order Correlators (OTOCs), alongside perturbative techniques like Feshbach-Fano projection.
model_or_system: The system is a mixed-field Ising spin chain coupled to a single spin-1/2 ancilla qubit. The Hamiltonian includes local interactions ($J$) and the tunable coupling ($\lambda$) between the ancilla and the chain's magnetization.
key_observables: Von Neumann entropy, Mutual Information saturation time, Out-of-Time-Order Correlator (OTOC) growth rate ($\log \alpha$), and state spread in Hilbert space.
important_parameters: The dimensionless ancilla coupling strength $\lambda$ acts as the primary tuning parameter controlling the dynamics between scrambling and confinement.
main_assumptions: The analysis contrasts emergent non-Hermitian dynamics (from tracing out the ancilla) with the closed, unitary dynamics of the isolated chain.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically shows the system and demonstrates how state spread changes from filling full space (weak $\lambda$) to being confined to specific subspaces like SU(2) Dicke states (strong $\lambda$).
paper_structure: The paper introduces the model, analyzes dynamics in different regimes ($\lambda$ weak vs. strong), quantifies the crossover using information measures (Mutual Information peak, OTOC suppression), and theoretically derives the confinement mechanism via symmetry arguments.
why_interesting: This work provides a clean, controllable platform to study fundamental transitions between chaotic/scrambling behavior and localized/confined dynamics using an engineered auxiliary degree of freedom, which is highly relevant for understanding quantum computation error correction or simulation protocols.
